title: ABAKADA to *MYBPM*
dek: A source-grounded reference guide to how a small Chicago Filipino streetwear label turned cultural fluency into product depth, community demand, and larger collaborations. It shows how MyBPM can adapt the operating principles without borrowing the identity.
sources: 9 web sources · 9 visual references · 5 MyBPM canon files

sections.heading: the *verdict*
sections.kicker: Study the operating engine, not the clothes
sections.body:
ABAKADA is a useful benchmark because its growth is legible. It began with a clear cultural premise, built a repeatable symbol vocabulary, expanded into more distinctive garment forms, and used bounded releases and collaborations to widen the world. The visible proof is longevity, repeated sell-through claims, a retail shop, and progressively larger partnerships. Revenue and profit remain unverified.

MyBPM should keep one permanent worldview: Raver as Identity Keeper / Night Society. Genres can act as seasonal lenses inside it. The first drop should stay ethos-led rather than genre-led. That preserves recognition, reaches more of the audience, and creates a clean baseline before house, techno, trance, bass, or drum & bass capsules change the texture.

Print-on-demand is the low-risk production bridge, not the final design ceiling. Waitlist interest chooses what deserves a paid pre-order. Paid orders fund production. Retained contribution after fulfillment pays for the next sample, custom silhouette, or tech pack.

rows.claim: The premise was culturally specific from day one.
rows.evidence: ABAKADA was founded in Chicago in 2018 by Arvin Boyon and Calvin Calma. The name comes from the traditional Filipino alphabet; the brand repeatedly uses Baybayin, the Philippine eagle, +63, jeepneys, sampaguita, language, and diaspora experience as design material.

rows.claim: The brand built a translation system, not a single logo trick.
rows.evidence: Across published product and editorial references, cultural codes move through minimal graphics, illustrative tees, lounge sets, sports jerseys, washed fleece, patchwork outerwear, knits, bottoms, and accessories. The source stays stable while the garment language evolves.

rows.claim: Pre-order and waitlist mechanics are part of the operating model.
rows.evidence: An official product page labels a distressed patch zip-up as PRE-ORDER and discloses a 4–6 week production/fulfillment window after the pre-order closes. An indexed password-gated storefront page asked visitors to join the waitlist while a collection was in production or fulfillment.

rows.claim: The growth path progressed from small-team fulfillment to broader cultural distribution.
rows.evidence: Multiple current profiles describe apartment-complex beginnings, collections selling out within hours, and a physical retail shop. Those are credible, repeated secondary claims, but no audited sales or profit data was found.

rows.claim: Collaborations compound the original story rather than replacing it.
rows.evidence: The 2023 DBTK collaboration connected a Chicago diaspora brand with a Philippine streetwear label. The 2024 Toyota/Complex/NTWRK project translated ABAKADA's visual language into anime and race-inspired merchandise. The output included a one-of-one letterman jacket. PENSHOPPE then announced a 23-piece Chicago-to-Manila collection for October 2026.

rows.claim: Out-of-stock labels are not the same as sales evidence.
rows.evidence: The official RESTOCK page showed 37 products as out of stock when indexed. That proves the merchandising state of the page, not why the inventory is unavailable, how many units existed, or whether the drop was profitable.

sections.heading: the visible *growth arc*
sections.tag: Selected milestones · Not a complete company history

items.title: Cultural premise locked
items.body: Founded in Chicago around a name and mission that could keep generating product: the Filipino alphabet as foundation, heritage as active design material.

items.title: Recognizable capsule vocabulary
items.body: Coverage highlighted minimal graphics, pastel and light shades, Baybayin, Filipino sayings, and named UBE and Forest collections. These were early signs of collection worlds rather than logo-only merch.

items.title: Diaspora-to-homeland collaboration
items.body: DBTK x ABKD joined Chicago and Philippine streetwear through shared graphics, exclusive colorways, tees, hoodies, shorts, and full-look styling.

items.title: Brand-world translation
items.body: Toyota GRIP moved ABAKADA into anime, racing graphics, heavyweight hoodies, premium patchwork, embroidery, and an extremely limited letterman jacket.

items.title: Product depth + pre-order discipline
items.body: The catalog shows outerwear, washed denim, mohair, fleece, knits, pants, accessories, and pre-order products with explicit fulfillment windows.

items.title: Scaled distribution without abandoning the premise
items.body: PENSHOPPE announced a 23-piece limited collection and an event pre-order before the full October launch. This is current as of Sep 1; the public launch has not happened yet.

sections.heading: visual reference *spine*
sections.tag: Study the decision · Do not reuse the image

items.title: Community as the hero
items.note: A recurring social unit, domestic props, restrained olive/cream/brown, and five distinct pieces create a world larger than a product grid. For MyBPM, use recognizable people across festival, club, and daily life instead of anonymous rave spectacle.

items.title: Graphic range inside one capsule
items.note: One look can be illustrative while another is typographic because fit, palette, styling choices, and cultural source keep them related. A MyBPM capsule does not need the same graphic pasted on every blank.

items.title: Collaboration as a new dialect
items.note: The eagle, paisley field, knit vest, shorts, oversized tees, and low-angle sky portrait make a full visual system. A MyBPM collaborator can change the capsule's dialect while Night Society remains the parent world.

items.title: A capsule reads as a set
items.note: Tees, tote, socks, and colorways share a phrase, palette, and graphic family while offering different commitment levels. For MyBPM, a hero garment, accessible tee, and low-risk object beat five equal tees.

items.title: Silhouette can carry the code
items.note: Raglan blocking, a crest, V-neck structure, side panels, and restrained marks create identity before a large back graphic is needed. As demand grows, MyBPM can shift some identity work from decoration into garment architecture.

items.title: Shape + application create perceived value
items.note: Cropped boxiness, drop shoulder, split lettering, patch application, and a clean product frame make a simple black zip-up feel considered. One MyBPM construction or placement decision should do more work than another layer of effects.

items.title: The world broadens into full looks
items.note: Varsity, cropped jersey, knit-neck top, fleece, baggy denim, skirt, and sweats show how a mature brand becomes wardrobe rather than merch. MyBPM should earn one new silhouette at a time until the customer can build a complete Night Society look.

items.title: Place gives the garment another layer
items.note: The Pilipinas jersey is photographed against riveted Chicago steel. The setting holds diaspora and hometown in one frame without adding explanatory copy. MyBPM can use transit, concrete, coat check, and first-light city locations with the same restraint.

items.title: Current MyBPM foundation
items.note: MyBPM already owns a stronger premise than generic EDM merch: identity after the wristband, the frequency below the floor, and product-proof gates. The gap is not a new story; it is richer cultural code, more varied product roles, and a demand-funded path to silhouette originality.

sections.heading: the MyBPM brand *architecture*
sections.dek: One permanent world; rotating lenses; product ambition earned by paid behavior.

items.why: The brand serves the person whose rave identity survives outside the event. PLUR beyond the dance floor, afterimage, found family, ritual, endurance, and return are the durable source material.

items.action: Seasonal capsule lens: ethos first, genre second
items.why: Capsule 001 should prove the broad identity. Later capsules may use house, techno, bass, drum & bass, or trance to alter motion, typography, material, and silhouette without creating separate brands.

items.action: Product ladder: signal → uniform → silhouette → artifact
items.why: Signal is an accessible tee or object. Uniform is the repeatable heavyweight core. Silhouette is the one new garment form. Artifact is the scarce, higher-craft piece that demonstrates where the brand is going.

items.action: One cultural code per hero piece
items.why: Use a coat-check number, wristband residue, transit time, water handoff, room stamp, set-time grid, or after-hours phrase as the single anchor. Layering every rave symbol at once becomes costume.

MYBPM wordmark, Signal White, Sublevel Ink, Mineral White, one Frequency Acid cue, sharp geometry, near-blank fronts, raster-backed statements, and no generic lasers/equalizers remain the recognition system.

sections.heading: how each genre changes the *dial*
sections.dek: The source is always the raver's lived experience. A genre only changes how that source is expressed.

items.why: Human proximity, shared motion, loops, warm flashes, relaxed knits or sport shapes, rounder typographic rhythm. Keep the direction away from predictable disco-ball imagery.
Functional pockets, modular placements, washed black, reflective micro-detail, narrow technical labeling, hard negative space. Keep these details functional instead of borrowing generic hazard tape.

Cropped outerwear, panel lines, transit maps, compressed type, asymmetric rhythm, sharp image slicing. Use the information density to organize the composition instead of covering it with random glitch overlays.
Translucent layers, edge light, optical trails, softer gradients, lifted proportions, white as atmosphere. Rainbow-neon nostalgia would flatten the idea.
Heavyweight fleece, low-center graphics, dense raster fields, oversized forms, sub-frequency diagrams, tactile decoration. Speaker and waveform icons are too literal.

sections.heading: recommended first capsule: *Afterimage Uniform*
sections.dek: A three-piece paid test that can be fulfilled through the existing POD bridge while creating one clear step toward original product.

items.why: Small exact MYBPM front; one photographic/raster back built around the moment the room ends but the body is still carrying the beat. DTG is the first sample path for tonal detail and transparency.
Quiet chest or split-seam mark, one sleeve/hood locator, oversized or drop-shoulder fit. It should feel like the garment someone reaches for after the venue, not event merch.

items.action: Signal object: cap, compact bag, or earplug case
items.why: A lower-commitment object widens entry without adding another large graphic tee. Choose only what can be sampled and fulfilled reliably now.

items.action: One experimental direction, shown but not produced
items.why: Reveal a cropped technical shell, paneled jersey, or custom trouser as the future artifact. Let waitlist preference and paid orders decide which tech pack earns funding.

The same cast and hero looks move through festival/open air, club/nightlife, and daily life/city. Afterimage is connective tissue: coat check, transit, food stop, and blue hour. It is not a separate gritty brand.

sections.heading: the pre-order *math*
sections.body:
Do not define success by gross sales. Per paid order, first reserve landed garment cost, decoration, packaging, transaction fees, subsidized shipping, taxes, and a refund/defect buffer. What remains is contribution; it becomes profit only after the order is fulfilled and all obligations are covered.

Minimum paid units = ceiling((sample + photography + setup + contingency) ÷ contribution per unit). Example only: if fixed launch cost is $600 and true contribution is $24 per paid order, the drop needs 25 paid units to cover those costs. At a modeled 15% waitlist-to-order conversion, that implies roughly 167 qualified waitlist members. The conversion rate is UNTESTED until MyBPM runs its first launch.

For the current POD bridge, collect full payment only on products whose supplier, sample, price, and delivery basis are known. For a future cut-and-sew experiment, use a refundable deposit or reservation until the factory quote, tech pack, sample, MOQ, and delivery range are real. Never spend the production reserve on content or the next capsule.

plays.title: Days 1–14 · Build the capsule card
plays.intent: Choose one lived rave ritual, one emotional thesis, one hero graphic, three product roles, and the one unproduced future silhouette.
plays.command:
CAPSULE 001 / AFTERIMAGE UNIFORM
Source ritual: the room ends; the signal stays in the body
Hero code: [one specific object, time, phrase, or trace]
Products: hero tee / uniform layer / signal object
Future artifact: [one custom silhouette]
No-go: lasers, equalizers, generic festival slogans, five unrelated graphics
plays.receipt: One-page capsule card with every item serving a distinct role.

plays.title: Days 15–30 · Sample + proof
plays.intent: Order only the single hero sample after the cost is approved; evaluate fit, print, wash, delivery, and usable photography.
plays.command: PASS only if: listed fabric/weight is true; measurements are recorded; decoration is centered and durable; one wash creates no unacceptable shrinkage/cracking/twisting; front/back/detail/on-body images are usable.
plays.receipt: Sample status is PASS / REVISE / KILL with photographs and actual landed cost.

plays.title: Days 31–52 · Earn the waitlist
plays.intent: Release the story in chapters: source ritual, making detail, silhouette reveal, fit evidence, price band, and launch date.
plays.command: Collect: email or SMS / size / preferred product / acceptable price band / one sentence on what the piece means. Do not count social likes as qualified demand.
plays.receipt: A deduplicated qualified waitlist with product and size preference, not just follower growth.

plays.title: Days 53–60 · Seven-day paid pre-order
plays.intent: Open and close the order visibly. Show the product, sample evidence, price, exact pre-order close, reasonable ship basis, and status-update cadence.
plays.command:
Pre-order closes: [date/time]
Estimated ship window: [supplier-supported range]
You will receive: order confirmation + weekly production update
If the window changes: consent to delay or cancel for a full refund
plays.receipt: Paid orders, size curve, contribution reserve, and refund obligations are reconciled before production.

plays.title: Days 61–90 · Fulfill + choose the next rung
plays.intent: Treat fulfillment as part of brand world-building; show production truth and decide which product earns development next.
plays.command: Review: paid units / gross collected / landed costs / refunds / defects / on-time rate / retained contribution / most-requested future silhouette.
plays.receipt: One fulfillment report and one funded next-product decision; no automatic expansion.

sections.heading: internal decision *blocks*
sections.tag: Copy into the next MyBPM session

blocks.label: Capsule generation brief
blocks.text: Create one MyBPM Night Society capsule from a lived rave ritual, not a genre moodboard. Preserve the MYBPM wordmark, Signal White / Sublevel Ink / Mineral White / one Frequency Acid cue, near-blank fronts, and one strong back statement. Produce exactly three sellable product roles: hero, uniform, and signal object. Add one unproduced future silhouette. Use the selected genre only to change pacing, material, typography, and shape. Reject lasers, equalizers, generic waveform art, festival slogans, and copied streetwear layouts.

blocks.label: Go / no-go check
blocks.text: Do not open paid pre-orders until one sample passes, landed cost and contribution are known, the supplier supports the advertised ship window, product/size preference is collected, and the minimum paid-unit threshold is calculated. Waitlist joins are interest. Paid orders are demand. Retained contribution after fulfillment is profit evidence.

blocks.label: Future silhouette gate
blocks.text: Choose one custom silhouette only when retained contribution can cover the quoted tech pack and at least two sample rounds without touching production reserves, and when paid demand concentrates around a clear product/fit request. Build one new form, not a collection.

sections.heading: what this guide *cannot prove*
sections.body:
ABAKADA's revenue, margins, team size, production contracts, exact launch funnel, customer acquisition cost, waitlist conversion rate, refund rate, and inventory financing are UNCONFIRMED. Secondary reports of fast sellouts and apartment beginnings are credible but not audited. The official out-of-stock page does not prove how many units sold.

The PENSHOPPE collection is announced for October 2026; as of Sep 1, 2026, the launch and its market outcome are future events. Visual references are used for internal analysis only. Rights remain with ABAKADA, PENSHOPPE, DBTK, the photographers, and their publishers; do not reuse them in MyBPM campaigns.

The FTC rule requires a reasonable basis for an advertised shipping time. If shipment is delayed, the customer must be offered a choice to consent to the delay or cancel for a prompt refund. Shopify also requires a pre-order app and supports full, partial, or no payment depending on the setup. This guide is operational research, not legal advice.
